speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Hey, this is Carlos, CEO at Product School and your host on The Product Podcast. My guest today is Jeetu Patel, President and Chief Product Officer at Cisco. Back for his fifth time on this show, he ran his own business for 17 years, then went inside a $63 billion company and calls himself a late-stage co-founder, 36 years late to the game. He also says Cisco has no product managers, only feature managers, and he means that as a strategy. Here are the things we'll cover: founder mode at Cisco scale, and why it annoys functional people; holding company to platform company after 250 acquisitions; agents past humans in token use, and what that breaks; when you can build anything, what you don't build is the job; and his 15-year-old daughter's hoodie startup, and the pricing lesson in it. Let's get into it. [Sponsor]  AI helps us generate ideas, draft plans, and spin up work in minutes. But faster doesn't necessarily mean better. When everyone has their own AI tools, their own outputs, and their own context, you get fragmentation: fractured version control, scattered review processes, decisions happening in parallel, not in concert. Rebuilding context between people and platforms costs you time and momentum. That's where Mural comes in. Mural gives teams a shared visual canvas to bring work together. You can generate structured starting points right on the canvas instead of moving outputs between tools, keep all of your context in one place, and compatible AI agents can contribute alongside the team, bringing in context from the tools they already know. The future of work is still human. Learn more at mural.co. Back for the Fifth Time

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: You're back by popular demand.

speaker: Jeetu Patel
text: I'm back. How many times is it? Fourth? Fifth?

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Fifth time.

speaker: Jeetu Patel
text: Fifth time. Wow.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Thank you. You've been supporting us since the very beginning. Even before you joined Cisco, you were still a CPO at Box.

speaker: Jeetu Patel
text: I tell you, your team flatters me. Because if Jeetu weren't in this business, you'd be an actor. There's no way. Who's going to give me a job, a bald, fat Indian guy? How many of those have you seen working?

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Quite a few, actually. Founder Mode at Cisco Scale

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: One of the things I want to cover with you is this concept of founder mode. As a startup founder, I actually run my company in founder mode, which is not easy, but it seems like you're also encouraging this type of founder mindset at a much larger scale. So I'm curious about how you actually make it happen.

speaker: Jeetu Patel
text: For 17 years of my career I ran my own business, and then I went to a very large company. What I found is there are two kinds of people. There are functional managers who are very, very good at making sure they can run their function well. And then there are people with an owner mentality who run their business. By the way, you need both. It's not like one is better than the other. I'm clearly the latter. I've always had an owner mentality. But if you're an owner mentality, you can tend to annoy a lot of functional people, because what the functional people want is to stay in the swim lane. You stay in your swim lane, I stay in my swim lane. I'll run my function, you run your function, and we'll go at it that way. Owner-mentality people poke their nose into everything. "This is not working for the business. I don't really care whose function it is, I'm going to go tell them it's not working, because we've got to fix it so we can win in the market." It annoys the hell out of the people on the functional side of the house. So you have to make sure that if you make the cultural change, you make it very explicit that we value an owner mindset. At Cisco, we've actually done that. We've said we value an owner mindset. So when you think about this, don't think from your function and your silo. I think of myself as a late-stage co-founder of Cisco. I was 36 years late to the game, but it's my company. Especially at a time when you're in wartime mode, when things are moving, you're having a platform shift, everything is changing, and you're refactoring your entire business, it's very hard to be in a functional mode and actually win in the market. So what you want to be is complete owner mentality, founder mode. When you make a decision to go to a company, try to assess which mode they're operating in. If it's a mode you don't actually value, don't go there, because you'll find yourself superbly frustrated all the time, unless you have enough agency to change the mode. From Holding Company to Platform Company

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I want to connect that to what you just said: war mode versus peace mode. It seems like a couple of years ago you went through an important org redesign. Instead of the traditional business-unit design, you went into a more platform, cross-functional design. That's a big change. A lot of people are trying to do it. How do you do it? What are some of the breaking principles that articulate this type of change?

speaker: Jeetu Patel
text: In large companies, the majority of things you cannot do by top-down dictation. But there are a few things you have to find religion in, and for those you cannot look for bottom-up buy-in. You have to just go drive it. In this particular case, we used to look like a holding company. We had done 250 acquisitions. Everyone wanted to be a GM. They thought the way to progress in their life was by being a GM. The problem with the GM is every GM wants their own sales, their own marketing, their own product, their own engineering. They don't want to talk to everyone else. They just want to keep growing their pie. And before you know it, you're not a $63 billion business, you're a collection of $100 million businesses. It's incomprehensible for the customer when you take $63 billion and divide it by $100 million, because you've got way too many businesses, and your go-to-market distribution channels can't make any sense of what you're trying to sell. So we had to move from being a holding company to being a platform company. A platform company means your priority has to shift from building a feature in a single product to making sure you become part of the larger platform. The way I tell people is: we don't have any product managers at Cisco. We have feature managers. We build features for the platform, and the platform is what we sell. We don't sell individual products. If you can do that right, you can shift the entire dynamic of how customers consume your product. One of the biggest reasons startups fail is not because they didn't build the right product. It's because they didn't understand how to drive it through a distribution channel. If you build a company, you build a product, you have extreme success, and now you say, "I want to become a multi-product company," what do you do? You build a second product, and a third product. If the second product doesn't leverage the route to market you built with the first product, you're going to fail in the second product. You won't become a multi-product company, you'll stay a single-product company. It's very important that you don't create multiple routes to market, because you can only attack so many go-to-market motions at one time. When you go to a large company, they already have established routes to market. And if you say, "I'm going to read one too many TechCrunch articles and start building products in different routes to market that you don't have an attack vector into," you'll fail there. So it's extremely important that you drive your entire organization to leverage the distribution channel you have. Just because you have a sales team of 20,000 people doesn't mean you can sell anything with those 20,000 people. You can only sell, through those 20,000 people, to the buyers they have access to. For the buyers they don't have access to, if you sell it, you're at a disadvantage compared to a startup, because you've got all of the weight of a large company but none of the agility of a small one.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Because right now you're at over $460 billion market cap.

speaker: Jeetu Patel
text: Whatever it is today.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: And over $63 billion in revenue.

speaker: Jeetu Patel
text: $63 billion in revenue last year. This year the guidance will be north of $70 billion. Making Acquisitions Become Team Cisco

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: So as you look at the breakdown, you make a lot of acquisitions. How do you make sure that integration goes as smoothly as possible, so they actually become Team Cisco?

speaker: Jeetu Patel
text: We've dialed down the number of acquisitions we make, because one of the challenges we had at Cisco was that most people would tell me, "Hey Jeetu, this seems like a very important market, what are we going to buy?" And that seemed like the wrong question, because you should never base your strategy on your acquisition strategy. So now, when they come to me and say, "Jeetu, this seems like an important market," I say, "What are we going to build?" Now, that doesn't mean that if you have a true north you've defined, and a company comes along that can accelerate you in achieving your vision, we would be shy to deploy our balance sheet. We wouldn't be. One of the largest acquisitions Cisco made was under my watch, with Splunk. But the strategy is not to be acquisitive. The strategy is to be very clear on what we're going to build, and if something comes along that accelerates our end-state vision, we won't be shy to deploy the balance sheet. Otherwise, we're just going to keep building. That also gives you a lot more mental peace, because you're not desperate, thinking, "oh my goodness, we've missed this market, now we need to go desperately buy someone." The only time I look to buy someone is if the founders are committed to taking on a larger vision, where they're going to join me in solving the problem we've encountered at Cisco. When we acquire a company, the first thing we do is kill their brand. We try not to keep the brand. There are exceptions, like Splunk, we've kept the Splunk brand because it's such a good brand, but most small companies, and I prefer buying small companies rather than large ones, we'll kill the brand, integrate it into the platform, and I take the founders and give them a larger mission. The mission typically would not be just to go take your company and do something with it. I always tell the founders, don't try to make your company a $100 million company within Cisco. Try to make Cisco a $5 trillion company. What are you going to do to make that happen? That gives them a larger aperture. They ask me, "Why should I stay at Cisco?" One of the big reasons to stay at Cisco is that if you stay for a four- or five-year period, my commitment to them is I'll make you a better operator than you could ever have been if you weren't working at Cisco. You'll understand at-scale motions. You'll understand how to run things in a way where you're running like the world's largest startup, so that the next time you become a CEO, you'll be far more successful than you would have been had you not worked at Cisco. That's the commitment we make to them. So far, I've personally made about 28 acquisitions. There was one company where the CEO was a jerk and it didn't work out well. 27 of them worked out pretty well. The way I've configured my team is a rule of thirds. One third of the people are very good at navigating Cisco. They're consummate operators, they know how to navigate Cisco. The other third we get from the industry, systems thinkers who know the industry and the markets we're in pretty well. And the final third are CEOs of startups I bring in, to work with the other two constituencies but break glass and do things we wouldn't otherwise be able to do, operating in complete founder mode. If I look at one of my key guys, DJ Sampath, who used to run a company called Armorblox, we got him, we killed the product, we killed the brand, but he's actually running our biggest platform and AI initiatives right now. He's running all AI and all platform for all of Cisco. The guy was running a 20-person outfit, but he's becoming such a great operator that, hopefully he'll never leave, but when he does leave, he'll be a much better CEO than he would have been had he not been at Cisco. That's the promise you want to deliver.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: As a fun fact, I met someone today from Cisco's leadership team who said she had an offer on the table, came to ProductCon last year, heard you speak, and ended up joining your company because of you, that type of energy that is so hard to find in a large enterprise.

speaker: Jeetu Patel
text: That's great. I'm hoping that person is still there, otherwise it would be an awkward moment. But I think we're lucky, because we've got a fantastic mission. Every once in a while you find a company where the body of work you do is going to shape the lives of billions of people and shape the way the world operates, and Cisco happens to be at that point right now. We've got the right amount of scale, but a tremendous amount of ceiling to grow. I'm hoping the people at Cisco right now, in the next five to ten years, are going to do their life's best work at Cisco. I'm pretty sure they will, because we're going to be doing some crazy stuff in the next few years. Agents Past Humans in Token Use

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Let's talk about some of the AI crazy stuff going on right now. I think we're at the beginning of another supercycle. We're seeing more agents using the internet than actual humans, and all these new AI assistants. So what does that mean for Cisco and the products, from a security and safety perspective?

speaker: Jeetu Patel
text: Let's look at the stats. Sub-2% of the world is using agents in any kind of power-user capacity today. My prediction is that in the next 12 to 15 months, you'll have about 30 to 40% of humans using agents in a power-user capacity, not AI as in chatbots, but delegating work, long-running-horizon tasks, to agents. That's number one. Number two: in February of this year, agents surpassed humans in token consumption. By August, agents' token consumption had grown 14x, and it's now five times that of humans. So when you start to think about the exponential curve agents are on, these agents work 24/7, they're going to keep working. 60% of the world's compute, by the end of 2026, is going to be consumed for inferencing capability, not for training. Scaling laws and training still apply, and people are going to spend much more on training than ever before, so the growth rate for training has not slowed down, but the ratio between training and inference has way surpassed training. What does that tell you? It means agents and AI are actually working. People are using it. The biggest challenge you're going to have is one of safety and security. People are going to be concerned with it. The second big challenge is that we're going to be supply-constrained: not enough compute, not enough power, not enough network, not enough data center capacity for the foreseeable future, the next five, seven, ten years. We happen to be in both those businesses. I think personal agents are going to be the next ChatGPT moment in the market. But here's what's going to be really interesting with agents: you will have an enormous amount of pressure as a business to understand the business-model shifts that are going to happen as a result of the disruption agents will cause. Let me give you a very simple example. Assume you're a retailer, and you've enjoyed a direct relationship with your consumer. You have a website. They come to your website, you've got advertising, upsell, cross-sell. You have a store, they can come to your store. Everything's great. All of a sudden, as a human, you've delegated the job to an agent. So it's the agent that's going to talk to the website, which means the agent is not going to be succumbing to cross-sell and upsell quite the way you are. And even if the brand gets smart enough to do that, you now have an intermediary between the brand and the consumer, which is the agent. So there are going to be profound shifts in business models. When You Can Build Anything, What You Don't Build Is the Job

speaker: Jeetu Patel
text: My point is, you will have a profound shift in business models. Whenever there's a big shift in business models, when you go from direct to indirect, when there's an intermediary, when there's disintermediation of the middleman, that creates a lot of opportunity for wealth creation, but it also means a lot of disruption. And by the way, the third phase, physical AI, robotics and humanoids, is already here. If you go to any of the semiconductor fabs, if you go to Taiwan and talk to TSMC, there's a ton of robotics work going on all around the world. So what you're going to start to see is that we, as product people, have to get very good at figuring out what kind of product-management evolution needs to happen in the world of AI that's different from the world pre-AI, and especially in the world of agents. What you can't do is get intellectually lazy and just delegate work to an agent. What you have to do is get intellectually superior by using an agent to boost your thinking. Right now, I think there's a lot of slop. If you can do one thing when you walk out of here: don't contribute to the slop. Contribute to the distillation and clarity people have. Because in a world where you could code anything, what you choose not to build is far more important than what you choose to build. And what you choose not to build requires judgment. It requires taste. It requires instinct. It requires a visceral understanding of the market and the customers. That is the job of the product manager, to direct that. It's an exciting time to be alive in tech. My daughter right now is 15 years old. If I had one secret wish, it's that I wish she got into product, because there's so much opportunity. She's 15, and it was interesting: she and her boyfriend are starting a startup. She likes streetwear, so she's going to start a startup doing hoodies, t-shirts, sweats, that kind of stuff. Here's what she did at 15, and this blows my mind. She's not particularly tech-savvy, doesn't like coding, doesn't like any of the tech stuff. She's very good with social media and creativity, loves makeup. She built a website for hoodies. She designed the hoodies. She reached out to three companies, one in China, one in Vietnam, one in LA, for the manufacturing process. And then she was telling me about her pricing strategy. I'm like, "How much are you going to charge for these hoodies?" She said, "I don't know, dad, between $275 and $325." I'm like, "That's expensive." She said, "Dad, I'd rather sell a few units at a higher cost, because the profit margin is going to be higher. And sometimes if you charge higher, people think it's better." For 15, that's extremely sophisticated, to understand your pricing strategy. That's only possible because she used Lovable. She was able to build a website within 24 hours. She was able to design the products. And the fact that she had to reach out to suppliers to figure out who's going to manufacture these came from ChatGPT. She just understood the entire ecosystem so well. That's who the next generation is going to be. So we have to think about this in a very creative way, end to end, as a business. Product people have to think about the entire business. You can't think about it functionally. If there's one function that should be in founder mode all the time, it should be product management, because you have to think about sales, marketing, engineering, product management, pricing, packaging, finance, and accounting. Every single area has to be thought about as you build your products. So it's a great time to do this with AI. It also gives you a lot of disruptive ability to do things in a way you might never have imagined before. Use AI not just as a productivity boost. Use AI to do things that could never happen before. And one thing I'd ask: every PowerPoint deck these days, every product these days, looks the same. We don't want to become a world where AI has taken away all originality from people. You want to inject a level of creativity into this. Use AI to enhance our thinking, don't use AI to be intellectually lazy. Designing for Humans and Agents

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: So, Jeetu, one of the challenges I see in product is that your customer is not always a human. You just mentioned that many of your customers can be agents acting on behalf of humans. As you design an experience, it seems like today agents are pretending to be humans and kind of hacking the system, and then sometimes they get blocked. Amazon recently decided not to allow certain shopping agents to go and purchase stuff. So how are you thinking about designing those types of products for both humans and agents?

speaker: Jeetu Patel
text: This morning I was in Austin. We had our Webex event, and we just launched a bunch of agents and a personal concierge for every brand. So every brand can now have a personal concierge agent for every customer of theirs. Think about what agents are going to be able to do for you. It's going to give you complete personalization. If you work with Cisco, it'll give you safety and security. But the third thing it gives you is an intense amount of scale, because you're now not bound by human caps on how many people you can have as a personal concierge. Historically, you'd say my top 20 customers, my top 100 customers, are going to have a named account rep. Here, you're going to have every single customer, no matter how big or small, have a personal concierge. They'll be able to do everything from support to sales to consulting, anything you want them to do. So there's a business-model shift we have to fully internalize ourselves. If we do that right, the amount of economic opportunity that will exist is going to be at epic proportions compared to anything we've ever seen before. But it requires an entirely different way of thinking, and it requires that you don't become part of the herd. You become contrarian in your thinking. When everyone says go this direction, start thinking about going someplace else. But don't be contrarian just for the sake of being contrarian. Start to question why everyone is going that way. Typically, when you see herd mentality, there's not enough thought going into it. That's when you want to create counterintuitive thinking. In product management, that is the only way you can get an insertion point when there's an incumbent. Otherwise, the incumbent has the advantage. The way you get an insertion point is by creating counterintuitive thinking and creating asymmetry where there wasn't any. That's what creates a level of tempo and momentum. And tempo is contagious. Once you start winning, like at Cisco, no one thought six years ago, they thought I was nuts going to Cisco, "what are you doing, are you crazy?", but now there's a spring in the step of the employee base, and people call me from the outside and say, "Can I come join you?" You want to make sure you're building things that get your employee base proud. And the team that does that most effectively is a product management team that gets the entire company to feel the tempo. The brand and the momentum get felt, for better or worse, by how the product management team operates, because they create the long-running true north. If it's a lousy true north, no one's going to follow you, and everyone's going to be in a malaise. But if you create something exciting, everyone's going to love it. The excuse a lot of people have is, "I don't have a budget." Budget does not precede a vision. A vision precedes budget. So you always want to start with a vision. It's so easy these days to build product, because you can build a product with one or two people and a bunch of tokens, so don't let that hold you back. Make sure you have extremely discontinuous, asymmetric, creative thinking that gets injected. Staying in Tune With What's Coming Next

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: To bring the point home: you talk about judgment, operating in founder mode, trying to stay in touch with what's really going on, build instead of buy. But there's also a lot of legacy. You have a core business you have to run and keep the lights on. So how do you ensure that you stay in tune with what's coming next, so you can catch that next wave and not be a late adopter?

speaker: Jeetu Patel
text: So I have a rule. Every week I have dinner with one person outside of Cisco. The reason: I have only one objective in that dinner. I want to learn one thing I didn't know from that one person. I have enough questions for them that I can get one insight I didn't have prior to entering the dinner. And I need to make sure I can teach them one thing, so it's valuable for them as well. In large companies, and even small companies, we get very insular in our thinking. You become the sum average of the five people you spend the most time with. So keep changing the five people, and make sure all five are always, at all times, smarter than you on some dimension, because it's important that you learn from them. It energizes people when you learn. It depletes your energy when you don't learn, because then you start worrying about the stupid stuff that doesn't matter. When you're learning, you're just focused on learning. So I make sure I'm always in a learn-it-all mode, like Satya says. It's a great way to be, because if someone gives you feedback about something that's not going well, think about it this way: they care enough about you to tell you things that are deeply uncomfortable to them, because it's much easier to say that everything's great. If they come and tell you that something sucks and you're not doing a great job, it's only because they care. So if someone gives you negative feedback, preserve those people in your life, bring them into your life more often, welcome them, because that means they care. And seek them out. What I tend to do is make sure the people closest in my inner circle don't give me false flattery. They tell me when something's working, they tell me when something's not working, so I can constantly make sure I'm improving. All you have to do is be 1.27% better today than you were yesterday. If you do it for 365 days in a year, you're 100x better by the end of the year, because of the sheer power of compounding. It's just math. If you do that for two years, imagine what happens. Three years, imagine what happens. If you do it for a decade, imagine the disproportionate advantage you'd have over someone who's not thinking in that growth mindset. It's tremendously accretive. So that's the way I'd think about it.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: To many more years learning from you. Thank you again for being part of this. What a way to wrap up the day here at ProductCon.
